summary: The authors achieve energy resolution of 3.7 µeV at 10 mK in scanning tunneling microscopy by combining local electromagnetic shielding and low-pass filtering directly at the cryogenic scan head, improving spectroscopic precision by nearly an order of magnitude. The enhanced sensitivity reveals that the Josephson current couples to centimeter-scale cavity modes of the scan head, establishing a direct connection between atomic-scale tunneling and macroscopic cavity quantum electrodynamics.
motivation: At mK temperatures, dynamical Coulomb blockade fundamentally limits STM spectroscopic resolution through energy exchange between tunneling electrons and the electromagnetic environment, motivating engineering approaches to suppress this noise and access ultra-low-energy phenomena.
method: The authors installed $\pi$-filters on twisted-pair cables and coaxial low-pass filters (Basel Precision Instruments) directly at the cryogenic scan head and at room-temperature feedthroughs. The metallic scan head acts as a complete electromagnetic enclosure; they model the cavity using cylindrical waveguide theory and fit Josephson spectra using dynamical Coulomb blockade $P(E)$-theory with an environmental impedance parameterized as Lorentzian resonances.
result: Benchmark measurements using Josephson current switching voltage asymmetry yield 3.7 µeV energy resolution at 10 mK (improved from prior 10.6 µeV) and 14 µeV at 560 mK; fitting the spectrum identifies cavity modes with energies ranging from 14.91 µeV to 180 µeV, matching calculated $E_{nl} = \hbar c\sqrt{(x_l/R)^2 + (n\pi/L)^2}$ for cylindrical eigenmodes with deviations $\leq 7\%$ and quality factors $Q \approx 600$–4500.
